gloss: strive, quarrel; contend at law; plead a cause; strife, dispute, case
summary: To strive with another in words: a quarrel between herdsmen over a well, and above all a case brought before a judge, where one side contends against the other. So the verb is to quarrel, to bring a charge against someone, or to take up and plead someone's cause, and the noun רִיב is strife, a dispute, or the case itself. Yahweh brings his own רִיב against Israel and the nations, and as redeemer pleads the cause of the fatherless, the widow and his captive people. Meribah, “strife”, is the place where Israel contended with Moses and tested Yahweh.

words.gloss: strive, quarrel; bring a charge, contend at law; plead the cause of
words.summary: About sixty-five times, nearly all qal (also written רוּב, Jdg 11:25; Job 40:2). It is strife carried on in words, the speech of a quarrel or a lawsuit, though a quarrel may end in blows (Exo 21:18) and it stands beside “fight” (Jdg 11:25; Psa 35:1). With עִם or אֵת of the opponent it is to quarrel with or accuse; with לְ, or with the noun רִיב as its object, it is to contend for someone, to plead his cause. The brief's 74 tokens with no stem are the noun רִיב and the adjective רַב filed here by spelling; 1Sa 15:5 וַיָּרֶב is אָרַב “lie in wait”.

stems.gloss: quarrel, strive with; bring a charge against, contend at law; plead the cause of

senses.definition: Of people at odds: to dispute with words, angrily, over a right or a wrong, with עִם or אֵת of the other side.

evidence.note: “The herdsmen of Gerar וַיָּרִיבוּ with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, The water is ours”; the well is named Esek, “contention”.
Jacob was angry “וַיָּרֶב with Laban”: what is my trespass, what my sin?
“When men יְרִיבֻן and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist”: a quarrel that comes to blows.
The men of Ephraim “contended with him sharply (בְּחָזְקָה)” for not calling them to the war.
“Did he ever strive (הֲרוֹב רָב) with Israel, or did he ever fight (נִלְחֹם נִלְחַם) against them?”
“Do not contend (תָּרִיב) with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm.”
Nehemiah “contended with the nobles and the rulers” over the usury taken from their brothers.
“וָאָרִיבָה with the rulers and said, Why is the house of God forsaken?”
Nehemiah contended with the men who had married foreign women, cursed them and struck some of them.
“The people וַיָּרֶב with Moses and said, Give us water … Why do you contend with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”
“These are the waters of Meribah, where the sons of Israel רָבוּ with Yahweh”: the quarrel with Moses was a quarrel with Yahweh.
Of Levi: “whom you tested at Massah, with whom you contended (תְּרִיבֵהוּ) at the waters of Meribah.”
“Woe to him who strives (רָב) with his Maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the ground! Shall the clay say to its potter, What are you making?”
Paul takes up Isa 45:9: “Who are you, O man, who answers back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why did you make me thus?”

senses.gloss: bring a charge against, contend at law
senses.definition: To take a case against someone, as in court: to accuse, to argue one's side against the other, and to seek a verdict. Used of Yahweh's case against his people, and of a man who would argue his case with God.

evidence.note: “Yahweh stands up לָרִיב, and stands to judge (לָדִין) the peoples.”
“Therefore I will yet contend with you (אָרִיב אִתְּכֶם), declares Yahweh, and with your children's children I will contend.”
“Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me.”
“Contend with your mother, contend, for she is not my wife”: the charge against an unfaithful wife.
“Arise, contend (רִיב) before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.”
“I will not contend (אָרִיב) for ever, nor will I always be angry, for the spirit would faint before me, and the breaths (נְשָׁמוֹת) I have made.”
“He will not always contend (יָרִיב), nor keep his anger for ever.”
“The Lord Yahweh was calling to contend (לָרִב) by fire.”
“He who justifies me is near; who will contend with me (מִי־יָרִיב אִתִּי)? Let us stand up together; who is my adversary at law (בַעַל מִשְׁפָּטִי)?”
Paul takes up Isa 50:8: “Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns?”
“If he wished to contend with him (לָרִיב עִמּוֹ), he could not answer him one in a thousand.”
“Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend with me.”
“Who is he who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.”
“Shall a faultfinder contend (הֲרֹב) with the Almighty?”
“If I despised the right of my servant or my maidservant בְּרִבָם עִמָּדִי”: when they had a case against me.
“Righteous are you, Yahweh, when I contend with you; yet I would speak with you of judgments.”

senses.definition: To take up another's case and argue it for him: the judge or redeemer who defends the weak against those who wrong them. Often with the noun as its object, רִיב רִיב “plead a cause”, and beside שָׁפַט “judge, vindicate” and גָּאַל “redeem”.

evidence.note: “Seek justice, set right the oppressor, judge (שִׁפְטוּ) the fatherless, plead for (רִיבוּ) the widow.”
“Yahweh be judge and judge between me and you, and see, and plead my cause (וְיָרֵב אֶת־רִיבִי), and vindicate me from your hand.”
“Blessed be Yahweh, who has pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal.”
“Contend, Yahweh, with those who contend with me (רִיבָה … אֶת־יְרִיבַי); fight against those who fight against me.”
“Judge me, O God, and plead my cause (וְרִיבָה רִיבִי) against an ungodly nation.”
“Arise, O God, plead your own cause (רִיבָה רִיבֶךָ).”
“Plead my cause and redeem me (וּגְאָלֵנִי); give me life according to your word.”
“For Yahweh will plead their cause, and rob of life those who rob them.”
Of the fatherless: “their redeemer (גֹאֲלָם) is strong; he will plead their cause against you.”
“Their redeemer is strong, Yahweh of armies is his name; he will surely plead their cause (רִיב יָרִיב אֶת־רִיבָם), that he may give rest to the land.”
“Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you.”
“You have pleaded, Lord, the causes of my soul (רִיבֵי נַפְשִׁי); you have redeemed my life.”
“I will bear the indignation of Yahweh, for I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me.”
“I will contend with him who contends with you (יְרִיבֵךְ), and I will save your children.”
“Your God who pleads the cause of his people.”
Joash: “Will you contend for Baal (תְּרִיבוּן לַבַּעַל)? … If he is a god, let him contend for himself.”

stems.gloss: contend with, be an opponent of

senses.definition: Only as a participle: those who contend with someone, his opponents.

evidence.note: “Yahweh: those who contend with him (מְרִיבָיו) shall be broken; against them he will thunder in the heavens.”
“Let no man contend (יָרֵב, qal) and let no man reprove, for your people are like those who contend with a priest (כִּמְרִיבֵי כֹהֵן).”

greek.gloss: judge; (middle, passive) go to law, contend

evidence.locator: Isa.49.25, אָרִיב → κρινοῦμαι; Jer.50.34, יָרִיב → κρινεῖ; Pro.22.23; 1Sa.25.39; Isa.50.8 (τίς ὁ κρινόμενός μοι, aligned to בַעַל מִשְׁפָּטִי); κρίνω and its forms render רִיב about fourteen times

evidence.note: “Brother goes to law (κρίνεται) with brother”: the lawsuit between brothers.
“If anyone wants to go to law with you (κριθῆναι) and take your coat, let him have the cloak also.”

parallels.note: Strive in words beside fight in arms.
Plead a cause beside judge, vindicate.
The one who pleads the cause is the redeemer.
Contend beside reprove, argue a case.

phrases.gloss: plead a cause, take up someone's case

words.gloss: strife, quarrel; dispute, case, cause; controversy
words.summary: About sixty times. Strife between people, and the dispute that comes before a judge: the case each side brings and the cause someone takes up. Yahweh's רִיב is his case against his people or the nations.

senses.definition: Angry contention between people, set beside מָדוֹן “contention” and opposed to quiet and peace.

evidence.note: “There was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock”; Abram answers, “let there be no מְרִיבָה between me and you … for we are brothers” (Gen 13:8).
“A man of wrath stirs up contention (מָדוֹן), but one slow to anger quiets strife (רִיב).”
“Better a dry morsel with quietness (שַׁלְוָה) than a house full of feasting with strife.”
“The beginning of contention is like letting out water; so quit before the strife breaks out.”
“It is an honour for a man to keep aloof from strife (שֶׁבֶת מֵרִיב), but every fool will be quarrelling.”
“Like one who takes a passing dog by the ears is he who meddles in strife not his own.”
“The pressing of anger brings forth strife.”
“Behold, you fast for strife and contention (לְרִיב וּמַצָּה), and to strike with the fist of wickedness.”
“Plundering and violence are before me; there is strife (רִיב), and contention (מָדוֹן) arises.”
“I have seen violence and strife in the city.”
“You hide them in a shelter from the strife of tongues.”
“You delivered me from the strivings of my people” (also Psa 18:44).
Jephthah: “I and my people were men of great strife (אִישׁ רִיב) with the sons of Ammon.”
“Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and a man of contention (אִישׁ רִיב וְאִישׁ מָדוֹן) to the whole land.”
The place was named Massah and Meribah “because of the strife (רִיב) of the sons of Israel, and because they tested Yahweh”.

senses.definition: A matter in dispute between two parties brought to a judge for a verdict; the case one side argues, or the cause someone takes up for another.

evidence.note: “If there is a dispute between men and they come to judgment, and they judge them, they shall justify the righteous and condemn the wicked.”
“If a matter is too hard for you in judgment … matters of dispute (דִּבְרֵי רִיבֹת) within your gates, then arise and go up to the place Yahweh chooses.”
“Both men between whom the dispute is shall stand before Yahweh, before the priests and the judges.”
By the word of the priests “shall every dispute and every assault be settled”.
“How can I bear alone your burden and your strife?”
“Do not answer in a dispute (רִב) to turn aside after the many to pervert justice; nor favour a poor man in his dispute.”
“Do not pervert the justice of your poor in his dispute.”
Absalom: “Every man who has a dispute and a judgment (רִיב וּמִשְׁפָּט) would come to me, and I would do him justice.”
Jehoshaphat set Levites, priests and heads of fathers “for the judgment of Yahweh and for disputes”.
“In a dispute they shall stand to judge.”
“The first to state his case (בְּרִיבוֹ) seems right, until his neighbour comes and examines him.”
“Argue your case with your neighbour, and do not reveal another's secret.”
“Present your case (רִיבְכֶם), says Yahweh; bring forth your strong arguments.”
“The men of your strife (אַנְשֵׁי רִיבֶךָ) shall be as nothing.”
“Listen to the pleadings (רִבוֹת) of my lips.”
“I was a father to the needy, and the case of one I did not know I searched out.”
“They do not judge the fatherless, and the widow's cause does not come to them.”
“To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord does not approve.”
“To you I have revealed my cause.”
“Awake to my judgment (לְמִשְׁפָּטִי), my God and my Lord, to my cause (לְרִיבִי).”

senses.gloss: Yahweh's controversy, his case against a people
senses.definition: The case Yahweh brings against Israel for breaking his covenant, or against the nations, set out as in court before witnesses and ending in his judgment.

evidence.note: “Hear the word of Yahweh, sons of Israel, for Yahweh has a controversy (רִיב) with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, no kindness, no knowledge of God in the land.”
“Hear, mountains, Yahweh's controversy … for Yahweh has a controversy with his people, and with Israel he will argue (יִתְוַכָּח).”
“Yahweh has a controversy with Judah, and will punish Jacob according to his ways.”
“Yahweh has a controversy with the nations; he enters into judgment with all flesh; the wicked he gives to the sword.”
“For it is the day of Yahweh's vengeance, the year of recompenses for the cause of Zion (לְרִיב צִיּוֹן).”
“The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment (κρίσιν) to the Son”: the judgment of Yahweh's controversy given into the hand of the man he raised.
“He gave him authority to execute judgment (κρίσιν), because he is the Son of Man.”
“An oath for confirmation is to them an end of every dispute (ἀντιλογίας)”: the dispute settled before Yahweh (Exo 22:10–11; Deu 19:17).

parallels.note: The case and the judgment given on it.

words.summary: The noun of strife with the prefix מְ־, used of strife between brothers and of the congregation's contention with Yahweh in the wilderness; most of its uses are the place named from that strife (the next word).

senses.definition: A quarrel between those who should be at one, and the congregation's rebellious contention in the wilderness of Zin.

evidence.note: “Let there be no strife (מְרִיבָה) between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers.”
“You rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin, in the strife of the congregation (בִּמְרִיבַת הָעֵדָה).”

evidence.locator: Num.20.13, Num.27.14, Deu.32.51, Deu.33.8, Psa.81.8, Psa.106.32: מְרִיבָה → ἀντιλογία ×6 (“water of contradiction”)

evidence.note: “Consider him who endured such hostility (ἀντιλογίαν) from sinners against himself.”
“They perished in the rebellion (ἀντιλογίᾳ) of Korah”: the wilderness contention against Moses and Aaron.

words.gloss: Meribah, “strife”, where Israel contended with Yahweh
words.summary: Two places in the wilderness named for Israel's strife over water: at Rephidim, named Massah and Meribah (Exo 17:7), and at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, “the waters of Meribah” (Num 20:13), where Moses and Aaron did not sanctify Yahweh and were barred from the land. Ezekiel's land has its southern border at “the waters of Meribah of Kadesh”.

senses.definition: Massah and Meribah at Rephidim, and the waters of Meribah at Kadesh, both named for the people's strife with Moses and their testing of Yahweh.

evidence.note: “He called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the strife of the sons of Israel and because they tested Yahweh, saying, Is Yahweh among us or not?”
“These are the waters of Meribah, where the sons of Israel contended (רָבוּ) with Yahweh, and he was sanctified in them.”
Aaron shall not enter the land “because you rebelled against my word at the waters of Meribah”.
“Because you trespassed against me … at the waters of Meribah of Kadesh … because you did not sanctify me.”
“I tested you at the waters of Meribah.”
“Do not harden your heart as at Meribah, as on the day of Massah in the wilderness.”
Psa 95:8 quoted: “Do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion (ἐν τῷ παραπικρασμῷ).”
“They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses because of them.”
The southern border of the land “from Tamar to the waters of Meribah of Kadesh”.

evidence.locator: Psa.95.8 (LXX Psa 94:8), ὡς ἐν τῷ παραπικρασμῷ for כִּמְרִיבָה; not aligned word by word in MACULA

evidence.note: “Do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, as in the day of testing in the wilderness.”

words.summary: Three times, with a suffix: the one who contends with someone, his opponent in a case. The form is that of the qal imperfect “he contends” used as a noun, as in the name Jarib.

senses.gloss: opponent, one who contends with someone
senses.definition: The other side in a quarrel or case; the one Yahweh is asked to contend with.

evidence.note: “Contend, Yahweh, with my opponents (יְרִיבַי); fight against those who fight against me.”
“I will contend with your opponent (יְרִיבֵךְ), and your children I will save.”
“Give heed to me, Yahweh, and hear the voice of my opponents.”

words.gloss: Jareb, “contender”(?), a title of the king of Assyria
words.summary: Twice, in מֶלֶךְ יָרֵב, the king of Assyria to whom Ephraim sent for help and tribute. Pointed as the qal jussive “let him contend” (the form of Jdg 6:32; Hos 4:4), it would be a title, “king Contender”; but the consonants also divide as מַלְכִּי רָב, “the great king”, the Assyrian title, which would be another root (רבב). Its tie to ריב is not certain.

senses.definition: The title of the Assyrian king to whom Israel looked instead of to Yahweh, who could not heal them.

evidence.note: “Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to king Jareb (מֶלֶךְ יָרֵב), but he cannot heal you.”
The calf “shall be carried to Assyria as a present for king Jareb”.

cognates.gloss: shout, clamour, be in uproar; uproar, clamour
cognates.note: The Peshitta uses the noun for θόρυβος “uproar” (Mat 27:24), τάραχος “stir” (Act 12:18) and κραυγή “clamour” (Eph 4:31; Rev 21:4), and the verb at Act 24:9, where the Jews joined the accusation before Felix. The noise of a dispute fits the Hebrew's quarrel and lawsuit (Isa 58:4, “to make your voice heard”), but the Syriac never means contend at law, and the Peshitta does not use it for רִיב.

evidence.locator: lexeme 2965, RB (root 1739 RB), shout; uproar; Act 24:9
lexeme 2966, ROBA (root 1739), uproar; Mat 27:24, Act 12:18, Eph 4:31, Rev 21:4

cognates.gloss: disquiet, disturb the mind; make doubt, suspect; doubt, suspicion
cognates.note: The same consonants with a middle y, but the sense is disquiet and suspicion, not dispute. A link through a mind stirred up against another is possible but not shown.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1197, art. ريب, رَابَنِى (n17211)
evidence.note: “It (a thing) occasioned in me disquiet, disturbance, or agitation, of mind … it made me to doubt.”

cognates.note: A hollow root of the same consonants, of the earth or a person shaking. Agitation is the only meaning shared with the Hebrew, and that only loosely.

doctrine.statement: Yahweh is the one who pleads the cause of the weak: the widow and the fatherless, whose “redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause” (Pro 23:11; Isa 1:17), and captive Israel, whose redeemer “will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the land” (Jer 50:34). The psalmist asks, “plead my cause and redeem me” (Psa 119:154), and Jerusalem confesses, “you have pleaded the causes of my soul; you have redeemed my life” (Lam 3:58), and waits “until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me” (Mic 7:9). The servant whose back was given to the smiters says, “He who justifies me is near; who will contend with me?” (Isa 50:6, 8), and Paul gives those words to all who are in Christ: “Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom 8:33–34). So redemption is set out as a case at law that God himself takes up and wins for his people, through the Son he raised from the dead.

Yahweh brings his own case against his people for breaking his covenant: “Yahweh has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, no kindness, no knowledge of God in the land” (Hos 4:1), and he calls the mountains to hear it (Mic 6:1–2). He has a controversy with the nations too, entering into judgment with all flesh (Jer 25:31), and a year of recompense “for the cause of Zion” (Isa 34:8). Yet he does not contend for ever, “for the spirit would faint before me, and the breaths I have made” (Isa 57:16; Psa 103:9): man is breath that his maker sustains, and cannot stand in a case against him (Job 9:3). The clay has no case against its potter (Isa 45:9), as Paul answers the man who would argue with God (Rom 9:20).

At Meribah the sons of Israel contended with Moses and so with Yahweh, testing him with “Is Yahweh among us or not?” (Exo 17:2, 7; Num 20:3, 13). There Moses and Aaron did not sanctify Yahweh before the people, and for that they were not to bring the congregation into the land (Num 20:12, 24; Deu 32:51). The psalm warns, “Do not harden your heart as at Meribah … they shall not enter my rest” (Psa 95:8–11), and Hebrews applies it to believers: those who would not believe did not enter, and “there remains a sabbath rest for the people of God” (Heb 3:15–19; 4:9). The promised rest is still ahead, to be entered by faith, and the strife of unbelief shuts a man out of it.

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. Words: verb רִיב (t.cm.aa, with the zero-token cross-references t.ad.ao רִב and t.bh.ae רוּב), noun רִיב (t.cm.ab), מְרִיבָה noun (t.cm.ah, with cross-reference m.dm.ad) and place (t.cm.ai), יָרִיב “opponent” (t.cm.ae), יָרֵב (t.cm.ad). BDB keys and counts: t.cm.aa's 74 stemless tokens are the noun רִיב and the adjective רַב filed by spelling; its hiphil 1Sa 15:5 וַיָּרֶב is אָרַב “lie in wait” and its niphal Job 31:13 בְּרִבָם is the qal infinitive; 1Sa 2:10 מְרִיבָיו (hiphil participle) is not among the brief's tokens and is cited by hand, as is Pro 3:30 תָּרִיב. t.cm.ad counts Hos 4:4 יָרֵב (the verb); t.cm.ae and t.cm.af share verb tokens by spelling; t.cm.ah and t.cm.ai share their tokens. Names: Jerubbaal (t.cm.aj, with יְרֻבֶּשֶׁת t.cm.ak) and Merib-baal (t.cm.al) already have names/jerubbaal.json and names/merib-baal.json under baal and are left there, though both are formed with this verb (Jdg 6:32 spells it out); Mephibosheth (m.da.ay) is with bosh. New here: names/jarib.json (t.cm.af), names/ribai.json (t.cm.ac), names/jeribai.json (t.cm.ag), names/joiarib.json (e.az.ao, יְהוֹיָרִיב and יוֹיָרִיב). Jeroboam יָרָבְעָם (t.ae.aj, under רבב) may be “let the people contend” or “the people increase”; left for whoever settles its root. Zero-token j.dg.ac (יָרֵב as the names' verb) and m.dm.ac (מְרִי־בַעַל) left unclaimed. Cognates: no cognate found that means “contend, dispute”. Syriac rwb “clamour, uproar”, Arabic rāba “disquiet, make doubt” and Akkadian râbu “quake” are entered as possible only; the Peshitta renders רִיב with other roots (no Peshitta cognate root in the brief). Not consulted: Payne Smith and Brockelmann for Syriac rwb, CAD R for râbu, DULAT for Ugaritic, Ge'ez (Dillmann, Leslau), Jastrow and CAL for Jewish Aramaic (Jastrow's ריב entries are Mishnaic Hebrew). Open questions: (1) whether the root has any true cognate meaning “contend”, or the Syriac clamour should be taken as one; (2) whether יָרֵב of Hos 5:13; 10:6 belongs here or is מַלְכִּי רָב “great king” under רבב; (3) Isa 27:8 תְּרִיבֶנָּה is left under “quarrel” though its sense (“you contended with her by sending her away”) is disputed.
